title: Chess Basics
source_note: Written for HEARTH, August 2026. Piece movement, values, tactics names, famous openings and mate patterns, all described in words so no diagrams are needed.

questions.prompt: How many squares are on a chessboard?
questions.explanation: The board is 8 by 8, which makes 64 squares.

questions.prompt: Who moves first in a game of chess?
questions.explanation: White always makes the first move, which is a tiny head start.

questions.prompt: How many pieces (including pawns) does each player start with?
questions.explanation: Each side starts with 16: eight pawns, two rooks, two knights, two bishops, a queen and a king.

questions.prompt: How does a rook move?
choices: Any number of squares along a rank or file (straight lines)
questions.explanation: Rooks slide any distance horizontally or vertically.

questions.prompt: How does a bishop move?
questions.explanation: Bishops slide any distance along diagonals, so each one stays on its starting colour forever.

questions.prompt: Which piece can jump over other pieces?
questions.explanation: Only the knight jumps; everyone else needs a clear path.

questions.prompt: How does a knight move?
choices: Two squares one way, then one square at right angles (an L shape)
questions.explanation: The knight's L shaped hop makes it tricky, and it always lands on the opposite colour square.

questions.prompt: How does the queen move?
choices: Like a rook and a bishop combined
questions.explanation: The queen slides any distance in straight lines or diagonals, making her the strongest piece.

questions.prompt: How far can the king move on a normal turn?
choices: Any distance in a straight line
questions.explanation: The king steps just one square at a time, except for the special castling move.

questions.prompt: How do pawns capture?
questions.explanation: Pawns walk straight but capture diagonally, one square forward to the left or right.

questions.prompt: How many squares can a pawn move on its very first move?
questions.explanation: From its home square a pawn may step one or leap two squares forward.

questions.prompt: What happens when a pawn reaches the far end of the board?
choices: It is removed from the game
It promotes, usually to a queen
It must stop and stay there
questions.explanation: A promoting pawn becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight, and nearly everyone picks a queen.

questions.prompt: What is 'en passant'?
choices: A special pawn capture of a pawn that just moved two squares past it
questions.explanation: If an enemy pawn jumps two squares and lands beside your pawn, you may capture it as if it had moved one.

questions.prompt: In castling, which two pieces move on the same turn?
questions.explanation: Castling slides the king two squares towards a rook and hops that rook to the other side of him.

questions.prompt: Which of these makes castling illegal right now?
choices: Your king would pass through a square attacked by the enemy
questions.explanation: You cannot castle out of, through or into check, and king and rook must both be unmoved with clear space between.

questions.prompt: Using the usual point values, how much is a queen worth?
questions.explanation: The queen counts as about 9 points, the most valuable piece after the priceless king.

questions.prompt: How many points is a rook usually worth?
questions.explanation: A rook is worth about 5 points, more than a bishop or knight at about 3 each.

questions.prompt: Which two pieces are usually valued at about 3 points each?
questions.explanation: Bishops and knights, the minor pieces, are each worth roughly 3 pawns.

questions.prompt: What does 'check' mean?
choices: The king is attacked and must be made safe this move
A player has offered a draw
questions.explanation: Check means the king is under attack, and you must block, capture the attacker or move the king.

questions.prompt: What is checkmate?
choices: The king is in check and there is no legal way out, ending the game
Both players run out of time
A pawn reaches the last rank
questions.explanation: Checkmate ends the game on the spot; the king is attacked and nothing can save him.

questions.prompt: What is stalemate?
choices: A win for the stronger side
A draw: the player to move has no legal moves but is not in check
questions.explanation: Stalemate is a draw, which is why the winning side must be careful not to trap the enemy king by accident.

questions.prompt: What is a 'fork' in chess?
choices: One piece attacking two or more enemy pieces at once
questions.explanation: A fork attacks two targets at once, and knights are famous for forking king and queen.

questions.prompt: What is a 'pin'?
choices: A piece cannot safely move because a more valuable piece stands behind it on the same line
Trapping a knight in the corner
questions.explanation: A pinned piece is stuck shielding something more valuable behind it, like its king or queen.

questions.prompt: What is a 'skewer'?
choices: An attack on a valuable piece that, when it moves, exposes a piece behind it
A knight trapped at the edge
questions.explanation: A skewer is a pin in reverse: the big piece must move and you win the one hiding behind it.

questions.prompt: What is a 'discovered attack'?
choices: Moving one piece so another piece behind it suddenly attacks
questions.explanation: You move one piece out of the way and unmask an attack from the piece behind, sometimes with check.

questions.prompt: What is a 'sacrifice'?
choices: Giving up material on purpose to gain a bigger advantage
questions.explanation: A sacrifice trades material for something better, like an attack on the king.

questions.prompt: What is the fastest possible checkmate, needing only two moves by the loser?
questions.explanation: Fool's mate punishes terrible pawn moves; White plays f3 and g4 and Black's queen mates on h4.

questions.prompt: Scholar's mate is the classic four move attack. Which squares does it target?
choices: The f7 square (or f2 for Black), next to the king
The centre squares e4 and d4
questions.explanation: Queen and bishop gang up on the weak f7 pawn, so learn to spot it and defend.

questions.prompt: What is a back rank mate?
choices: Checkmate by a queen or rook on the home row, with the king fenced in by its own pawns
Mate in the middle of the board
questions.explanation: A rook or queen slides to the back row where the castled king is trapped behind its own pawns, so give your king an escape hatch.

questions.prompt: What is a smothered mate?
choices: A knight checkmates a king completely boxed in by its own pieces
Mate using every one of your pieces
Mate by advancing all eight pawns
questions.explanation: Only a knight can deliver it, because the trapped king's own pieces block every escape square.

questions.prompt: The opening 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 is one of the oldest known. What is it called?
questions.explanation: The Ruy Lopez is named after a 16th century Spanish priest and is still played at world championship level.

questions.prompt: Black replies to 1.e4 with 1...c5. Which famous opening is this?
questions.explanation: The Sicilian Defence is the most popular fighting reply to 1.e4.

questions.prompt: The Queen's Gambit starts 1.d4 d5 2.c4. What is White offering?
choices: A pawn, to lure Black's centre pawn away
questions.explanation: White offers the c pawn to pull Black's pawn off the centre; it is a gambit of a pawn, never the queen.

questions.prompt: Which opening begins 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4, aiming the bishop at f7?
questions.explanation: The Italian Game develops the bishop to c4, eyeing Black's weakest square, f7.

questions.prompt: Which four squares are considered the centre of the board?
questions.explanation: Controlling the central squares e4, d4, e5 and d5 gives your pieces the most reach.

questions.prompt: Which of these is good general opening advice?
choices: Develop your knights and bishops early and castle your king to safety
Bring your queen out on move two
Move the same piece many times
Push all your edge pawns first
questions.explanation: Fast development, centre control and early castling win far more games than early queen raids.

questions.prompt: In chess notation, what does O-O mean?
questions.explanation: O-O is kingside (short) castling and O-O-O is queenside (long) castling.

questions.prompt: In notation, why is N used for the knight instead of K?
choices: K is already taken by the king
It was a printing error that stuck
questions.explanation: The king claimed K, so the knight takes N.

questions.prompt: In serious games, what does the 'touch move' rule say?
choices: If you deliberately touch one of your pieces, you must move it if you legally can
You may touch pieces while you think
You must announce every check by touching your king
You lose if you touch the board
questions.explanation: Touch it, move it, so decide with your eyes and only reach out when you are sure.

questions.prompt: In 1997, world champion Garry Kasparov was beaten in a match by Deep Blue. What was Deep Blue?
questions.explanation: IBM's Deep Blue was the first computer to beat a reigning world champion in a match, a famous moment for AI.
